t_page_garvan_events_e002:
Events let one part of your app notify others without knowing who is
listening. Fire an event once; every registered listener runs — synchronously,
in order of registration, in the same thread.
t_page_garvan_events_e004: An event is a small value class derived from Garvan::Event:
t_page_garvan_events_e007: The listener body can do anything — write to the database, call a service, or dispatch a job (which is exactly what SendWelcomeEmailListener does, forwarding to AppJobs::SendTestMail).
t_page_garvan_events_e009: Listeners are called synchronously in the same thread; if one throws, subsequent listeners are still executed and fire() re-raises the first exception at the end.
t_page_garvan_events_e012: Unlike GARVAN_REGISTER_JOB, the event macro is fine: the event's dispatch key is taken from eventName() at runtime, not from the stringified type name.
t_page_garvan_events_e013: Providers are booted in main.cpp:56-60 in a fixed order — AppServiceProvider first (queue drivers), then JobServiceProvider, then EventServiceProvider. Listeners can safely dispatch jobs at boot time because jobs are already registered.
t_page_garvan_events_e015: See Events & Jobs walkthrough for an end-to-end curl-and-verify tour.

t_page_garvan_jobs_desc: Job classes, JobRegistry, JobDispatcher and the sync driver.
t_page_garvan_jobs_e002: Jobs are units of background work. Every job is a C++ class that derives from Garvan::Job. They can be triggered directly, from an event listener, or over HTTP through the admin API (which is what kalpasan job:dispatch uses internally).
t_page_garvan_jobs_e004: Override four things and provide one static factory:
t_page_garvan_jobs_e006: Register every user job in JobServiceProvider::register_(). Use JobRegistry::bind() directly with the short name from jobName():
t_page_garvan_jobs_e007: The macro GARVAN_REGISTER_JOB(AppJobs::MyJob) stringifies the whole token and registers the key as "AppJobs::MyJob", which then does not match jobName() or the short name kalpasan job:dispatch expects. See the fix in app/providers/JobServiceProvider.cpp:18.
t_page_garvan_jobs_e009: Anywhere in your code — controller, listener, or another job:
t_page_garvan_jobs_e010: The dispatcher routes the job to the driver named by job->connection(). Drivers are bound by service providers; today only "sync" is wired in the starter.
t_page_garvan_jobs_e012: SyncDriver runs the job inline in the calling thread. This is the default in Phase A and gives you the same call-and-return semantics as a plain function call — perfect for testing, low-throughput tasks, or pipelines triggered by an HTTP request. Async and database-backed drivers will slot into the same JobDispatcher API in later phases with no changes to your job classes.
t_page_garvan_jobs_e014: The bundled AppJobs::SendTestMail (app/jobs/SendTestMail.h:21) is a real, sendable job. Its handle() opens an SMTP session with libcurl, sends an HTML email using the MAIL_* block from .env, and logs the outcome to stdout. See Mail (SMTP) for the SMTP side and Kalpasan CLI for the job:dispatch verb.
t_page_garvan_kalpasan_e002: kalpasan is the project's command-line companion. It scaffolds models, controllers and services, runs migrations and seeders, and starts a development server with file watching.
t_page_garvan_kalpasan_e004: The binary lives at vendors/Garvan/kalpasan. A symlink at the project root makes it convenient to call:
t_page_garvan_kalpasan_e006: All commands respect the active .env file so they target the right database.
t_page_garvan_kalpasan_e008: These verbs talk to a running app via HTTP (libcurl). They read KALPASAN_ADMIN_URL (default http://127.0.0.1:9090) and KALPASAN_ADMIN_TOKEN from .env, then hit the bearer-guarded admin endpoints in routes/AdminRoute.cpp.
t_page_garvan_kalpasan_e009: AdminRoute refuses the request unless three conditions hold: KALPASAN_ADMIN_TOKEN is non-empty in .env, the request comes from loopback (127.0.0.1 or ::1), and the Authorization: Bearer <token> header matches. Otherwise you get a JSON error with status 401 / 403 / 503 (see routes/AdminRoute.cpp:55-82).
t_page_garvan_kalpasan_e010: See Jobs, Events and Events & Jobs walkthrough.
t_page_garvan_mail_desc: Real HTML mail sending over SMTP via libcurl.
t_page_garvan_mail_e002: The starter ships one real, sendable job: AppJobs::SendTestMail. Its handle() (app/jobs/SendTestMail.cpp:58) opens an SMTP session with libcurl, builds an RFC 822 message with an HTML body, authenticates, sends, and logs the result. Everything is driven by the MAIL_* block in .env.
t_page_garvan_mail_e011: tls, ssl, or smtps. ssl/smtps force implicit TLS regardless of port.
t_page_garvan_mail_e016: Values may be quoted with "..."; the job strips surrounding quotes before use.
t_page_garvan_mail_e018: 465 → implicit TLS (smtps://). Handshake happens before SMTP banner.
t_page_garvan_mail_e019: 587 → STARTTLS. The job uses smtp:// and forces TLS via CURLUSESSL_ALL.
t_page_garvan_mail_e020: Any other port with MAIL_ENCRYPTION=ssl or smtps → forced implicit TLS.
t_page_garvan_mail_e022: The RFC 822 message header is fixed to Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8 with 8-bit CTE, so the body field can contain arbitrary HTML including UTF-8 text:
t_page_garvan_mail_e024:
If a send succeeds according to libcurl but never lands in the inbox
(spam, greylist, silent rejection), flip verbose mode on temporarily:
t_page_garvan_mail_e025: Rebuild, restart, retry. You get the full TLS handshake plus the SMTP dialog on the server's stdout — EHLO, AUTH, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, and the final 250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as ....
t_page_garvan_mail_e026: Verbose SMTP logs leak sensitive headers and can hurt performance. Flip back to 0L before committing.
t_page_garvan_mail_e031: See Jobs for the job pipeline itself, and Events & Jobs walkthrough for an end-to-end example.
t_page_garvan_migrations_e002: Garvan ships a standalone migration tool called garvan-migrate. It reads SQL or JSON files from db/migrations/, applies them in version order, and records what's already been run in a tracking table.
t_page_garvan_migrations_e004: The tool reads its connection settings from the same .env file your app uses.
t_page_garvan_migrations_e006: Filenames follow <UTC YYYYMMDDhhmmss>_<description>.sql. Each file has two sections, marked dbmate-style:
t_page_garvan_migrations_e007: For per-backend variants append .<dbtype> before .sql — for example 20240501_create_posts.mysql.sql.
t_page_garvan_migrations_e009: Every up must have a matching down — the tool refuses to apply a migration without one. garvan-migrate down runs them in reverse order, one at a time.
t_page_garvan_migrations_e010: For MongoDB migrations the file body is one or more top-level JSON documents. Each one is sent to db.runCommand() in order.
t_page_garvan_models_e002: A model represents one database table. It carries metadata (table name, primary key, columns) and inherits query-builder methods from ORM::OModel.
t_page_garvan_models_e004: Place your models under app/models/. A minimal model:
t_page_garvan_models_e006: Builder exposes four relation helpers that OModel inherits:
t_page_garvan_models_e011: Each one schedules a join that gets resolved when you call get(). They mirror the relation API you may know from Laravel.
t_page_garvan_models_e013: The typed pipeline (Model::query<T>(), TypedQuery<T>) hydrates rows into real model instances and closes the full CRUD loop — load, mutate, save() emits an UPDATE keyed on the hydrated id:
t_page_garvan_models_e014: See ORM → TypedQuery for the full API surface, terminal cheat sheet, guards and BC notes.
t_page_garvan_orm_desc: The Garvan query builder and ORM model layer.
t_page_garvan_orm_e002: Garvan's data layer has two pieces. Builder generates parameterized statements through a per-database Grammar, then runs them through a DbClient. OModel is the base class your model objects extend to expose those builder methods directly.
t_page_garvan_orm_e004: The builder uses a fluent API. Each call returns the builder so you can chain conditions:
t_page_garvan_orm_e005: The query is parameterized end-to-end — user-supplied values flow through native PreparedStatement binding rather than string concatenation. SQL injection is not on the table.
t_page_garvan_orm_e008: Models extend ORM::OModel and declare their table name plus column lists:
t_page_garvan_orm_e010: Each driver provides a Grammar subclass that knows how to emit the right dialect:
t_page_garvan_orm_e015: MongoGrammar — produces Mongo commands rather than SQL.
t_page_garvan_orm_e016: The right grammar is picked automatically from DATABASE_TYPE. You won't normally touch these classes directly.
t_page_garvan_orm_e018: Since 2026-08-21 the ORM ships a typed pipeline that hydrates results into real model instances (populating attributes and id), enabling a full CRUD cycle on the loaded object without leaving type safety. The classical Model::where<T>(...)->first() (returning raw json) stays untouched for BC.
t_page_garvan_orm_e050: Guards. Bulk update() / remove() refuse to run without at least one where(...) clause (protection against accidental full-table writes). Model::remove() on an unhydrated instance (empty id) also throws.
t_page_garvan_orm_e051: Behind the scenes. Connection layers ship results as JsonValue::RawJson (a JSON string). TypedQuery parses that back into a walkable Object/Array tree via JsonValue::parse(std::string_view) (RFC 8259, dependency-free) and calls Model::hydrate(row) — populating attributes and setting id so the next save() naturally hits the UPDATE branch.
t_page_garvan_orm_e053: Alongside the classical API the vendor exposes a family of C++23-only surfaces (full BC preserved). Rebuilding libgarvan.a from source requires GCC 14+ or Clang 18+.
t_page_garvan_orm_e055: Errors on a wrong T are short and readable instead of pages of template noise.
t_page_garvan_orm_e057: Terminal methods (get, find, first, …) no longer delete this. Stack instances are safe. Models returned from static where<T>() live in a thread_local scratchpad, cleared on the next where<T>() on the same thread or via an explicit Garvan::Model::flushScratch().
t_page_garvan_orm_e059: Concept-guarded overloads for integral / floating_point / bool / nullptr_t. The existing string API stays intact.
t_page_garvan_orm_e061: whereRef returns Self& instead of Self*, enabling value chains on stack builders. The old Builder* where(...) is kept for BC.
t_page_garvan_orm_e063: DbError::Code = { Connection, Syntax, Constraint, NotFound, Unknown }. Classification is currently heuristic (matched on what()); precise SQLSTATE-driven classification lands in a future connection-layer extension. Throwing methods stay for BC.
t_page_garvan_orm_e065: [[nodiscard]] on all query terminals and getters.
t_page_garvan_orm_e067: Operator allowlist is a constexpr std::array — no runtime heap allocation for the static set.
t_page_garvan_services_e002: Services sit between controllers and models. They hold business logic that doesn't belong in either — validation, multi-table operations, calls to external APIs.

t_page_garvan_services_e007: The service layer also makes testing easier — controllers become thin shims and services can be exercised without spinning up the HTTP server.

t_page_guides_app_desc: The SimpleApp / App class — the heart of Garvan.
t_page_guides_app_e002: A Garvan app is the object that ties the HTTP server, the router, the logger and any registered middlewares together. You'll see one in every project.
t_page_guides_app_e004: The most common choice is crow::SimpleApp. It has no middlewares attached at the application level — just routes.
t_page_guides_app_e006: When you need request-wide concerns (auth, sessions, CORS, etc.), reach for crow::App<M1, M2, ...>. The middlewares are composed left-to-right and unrolled at compile time.
t_page_guides_app_e008: The configuration methods are chainable, which keeps the entry point readable:
t_page_guides_app_e010: run() blocks the calling thread. If you need to keep doing other work, capture the handle returned by run_async() — let the variable fall out of scope and the server will shut down.
t_page_guides_auth_e002: HTTP authentication is performed through the Authorization header. Garvan does not impose a scheme; you read the header in a middleware or in the handler itself.
t_page_guides_auth_e005: JWTs and opaque tokens look the same on the wire:
t_page_guides_auth_e006: Pull the check into a middleware so it doesn't repeat in every handler. See the middleware guide.
t_page_guides_base64_e002: Base64 helpers come bundled in crow::utility. Use them for HTTP basic auth headers, embedded images, signed cookies, and similar tasks.
t_page_guides_base64_e005: Both functions are pure and allocate; they're fine to call inside handlers but reach for an arena allocator if you process megabytes per request.
t_page_guides_blueprints_e002: A blueprint is a group of routes that share a URL prefix, a template base, or a static directory. They're handy for splitting a large app into modules — for example one blueprint per API version.
t_page_guides_blueprints_e005: The blueprint's prefix is prepended to every route inside it, so the handler above answers GET /api/v1/users.

t_page_guides_compression_e002: Garvan can gzip or deflate response bodies on the fly. Enable it at build time and pick a default per app.
t_page_guides_compression_e004: Compile with -DCROW_ENABLE_COMPRESSION and link against zlib:
t_page_guides_compression_e005: Then turn it on per app:
t_page_guides_compression_e006: Clients that send Accept-Encoding: gzip will receive a compressed body; everyone else gets the response untouched.
t_page_guides_events_and_jobs_desc: End-to-end: fire an event, watch the job pipeline dispatch a real SMTP mail.
t_page_guides_events_and_jobs_e002:
This guide takes you from a single HTTP request to a real HTML email in
your inbox. It exercises every layer of the event / job pipeline in the
starter — event dispatcher, listener chain, job dispatcher, sync driver, and
libcurl SMTP transport.
t_page_guides_events_and_jobs_e004:
Nothing is queued to a background worker in Phase A — every step runs in
the request thread and the HTTP response only returns once the mail has been
handed off to the SMTP server. That means: if you get an HTTP 200, the mail
was accepted by the mail server; if the mail was rejected, the request
finishes with the error visible in the server log.
t_page_guides_events_and_jobs_e006: With ./bin/app.bin running and MAIL_* configured (see Mail (SMTP)):
t_page_guides_events_and_jobs_e009: In the terminal where ./bin/app.bin runs you should see, in order:
t_page_guides_events_and_jobs_e010: If you see SMTP send FAILED instead, the last line contains the libcurl error string — that is the actionable message.
t_page_guides_events_and_jobs_e012: 404 HTML instead of JSON — the running binary does not have the routes registered. Rebuild with ./make.sh and restart.
t_page_guides_events_and_jobs_e013: 404 JSON "no factory for '...'" — the job or event name in the URL / payload does not match any registered entry. Use ./kalpasan job:list and ./kalpasan event:list to see what is bound; check app/providers/JobServiceProvider.cpp and EventServiceProvider.cpp.
t_page_guides_events_and_jobs_e014: SMTP send OK but no mail in inbox — check spam folder first. If empty, flip CURLOPT_VERBOSE=1L in app/jobs/SendTestMail.cpp, rebuild, retry and read the full SMTP dialog (details).
t_page_guides_events_and_jobs_e015: Silent hang — the SMTP server is probably not answering. Try openssl s_client -connect <host>:465 from the same box; if it fails, network / firewall.
t_page_guides_events_and_jobs_e016: SPF / DKIM issues — first-time mail from a fresh domain to gmail.com, abv.bg, etc. is commonly filtered into spam. Configure SPF / DKIM / DMARC for your domain.
t_page_guides_included_middleware_e002: Crow ships a handful of ready-made middlewares; Garvan exposes all of them. Pull in whichever you need and add it as a template parameter to crow::App.
t_page_guides_included_middleware_e006: The session middleware is built on top of the cookie parser and stores arbitrary key/value data on the server side.
t_page_guides_json_desc: Reading and writing JSON with crow::json and Garvan's JsonValue.
t_page_guides_json_e002: Garvan reads JSON through crow::json::rvalue and writes it through crow::json::wvalue. There's also a thin wrapper JsonValue in the tools directory for use outside of request handlers.
t_page_guides_json_e004: Parse an incoming request body and access fields by key:
t_page_guides_json_e005: load returns a falsy value when parsing fails, so always check before accessing fields.
t_page_guides_json_e007: Build a wvalue and return it; Garvan sets Content-Type: application/json automatically.
t_page_guides_json_e009: JsonValue (alias json inside route headers) is a slim wrapper that adds a few conveniences for use inside services. The UserMysqlController in the bundled starter, for example, returns a JsonValue from its index() method.
t_page_guides_logging_desc: Crow's logger and Garvan's Logger helper.
t_page_guides_logging_e002: Garvan ships two logging facilities: Crow's built-in CROW_LOG_* macros, and a small helper class Logger in vendors/Garvan/include/tools/Logger.h.
t_page_guides_logging_e004: Crow's macros stream-style and respect a global level threshold:
t_page_guides_logging_e006: Use Logger inside service or model code when you don't have the Crow app reachable:
t_page_guides_logging_e009: Anything below Warning will be filtered out. In production you typically want Warning or Error; during development Debug is more useful.
t_page_guides_middleware_e002: A middleware lets you observe or mutate every request and response that flows through the app — auth, logging, CORS and sessions are typical use cases.
t_page_guides_middleware_e004: Each middleware is a struct with three things: a per-request context, a before_handle() hook called before the route runs, and an after_handle() hook called after.
t_page_guides_middleware_e007: Attach middlewares as template arguments to crow::App:
t_page_guides_middleware_e008: Inside a handler, retrieve your context with app.get_context<Timer>(req).
t_page_guides_multipart_e002: Browsers send multipart/form-data when a form contains file inputs. Garvan parses these requests through crow::multipart::message.
t_page_guides_multipart_e005: The body of each part contains raw bytes; write it out to disk:
t_page_guides_multipart_e006: Never trust the client-supplied filename. Strip path separators and validate against an allow-list before writing to disk.
t_page_guides_proxies_desc: Running Garvan behind nginx, Apache, or Caddy.
t_page_guides_proxies_e002: In production you'll usually run Garvan behind a reverse proxy that handles TLS termination, HTTP/2, request limits and static asset caching.
t_page_guides_proxies_e006: Caddy is the simplest of the three: it grabs a Let's Encrypt cert on first run and reloads it automatically.
t_page_guides_query_string_e002: Anything after the ? in a URL is parsed automatically. Access it via req.url_params.
t_page_guides_query_string_e004: get() returns a const char* or nullptr when the key is absent — always check before dereferencing.
t_page_guides_query_string_e007: For application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies (typical for HTML forms), call req.get_body_params() — the API is identical.
t_page_guides_routes_e002: A route binds an HTTP method + URL pattern to a handler. Garvan inherits Crow's compile-time router, which builds a decision tree from your route definitions — lookups are O(log n) and there's no regex involved.
t_page_guides_routes_e004: The canonical way to declare a route:
t_page_guides_routes_e005: You can also use app.route_dynamic("/hello") if you need to construct paths at runtime, but the macro form is preferred because it's checked at compile time.
t_page_guides_routes_e007: Place parameters in angle brackets and accept them as arguments to your handler. Supported types are int, uint, double, string and path:
t_page_guides_routes_e009: Routes default to GET. Use .methods(...) to register additional verbs:
t_page_guides_routes_e011: A handler can take zero or more arguments. The first argument may be const crow::request& to access headers and the body; the second may be crow::response& if you want to write the response incrementally and call res.end() yourself.
t_page_guides_routes_e013: Return a std::string for the body, or a crow::response when you need to set the status code or headers explicitly:
t_page_guides_routes_e015: Use CROW_CATCHALL_ROUTE(app) to define a fallback that runs whenever no other route matches. The docs site you're reading right now uses one to resolve unknown paths against a page index.
t_page_guides_ssl_e002: Garvan supports HTTPS through OpenSSL. You can run the server directly on TLS, or terminate it at a reverse proxy — see the proxies guide for the latter.
t_page_guides_ssl_e004: SSL must be enabled at build time. Add -DCROW_ENABLE_SSL to your compiler flags and link against OpenSSL:
t_page_guides_ssl_e006: Point the app at a certificate and private key:
t_page_guides_ssl_e007: If you only need development certificates, openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout privkey.pem -out fullchain.pem -days 30 -subj /CN=localhost produces a self-signed pair in seconds.
t_page_guides_static_desc: Serving static assets from the static/ folder.
t_page_guides_static_e002: Crow registers a route at /static/<path> that serves any file under the static/ directory of your project. Garvan inherits this for free.
t_page_guides_static_e004: Drop assets into static/css/, static/js/ or static/img/ and reference them in your templates:
t_page_guides_static_e005: The handler sets a correct Content-Type based on file extension and supports Range requests.
t_page_guides_static_e007: The directory and URL prefix are defined as compile-time macros in vendors/Garvan/crow/settings.h:
t_page_guides_static_e008: Override them before including crow.h if you need different defaults. For per-blueprint static directories, see Blueprints.
t_page_guides_systemd_desc: Run your Garvan app on boot using systemd.
t_page_guides_systemd_e002: To run your Garvan binary on boot, drop a systemd unit file in /etc/systemd/system/ and enable it.
t_page_guides_systemd_e005: The last command tails the logs — useful while you're setting things up.
t_page_guides_templating_desc: Returning HTML pages with mustache templates.
t_page_guides_templating_e002: Garvan exposes Crow's mustache implementation. The model is deliberately simple: a template file plus a context object equals rendered HTML.
t_page_guides_templating_e005: Page — a file on disk, loaded into a crow::mustache::template_t.
t_page_guides_templating_e006: Context — a crow::mustache::context (alias for crow::json::wvalue) carrying the values referenced by the template's tags.
t_page_guides_templating_e008: Templates live under a base directory. Set it once at startup:
t_page_guides_templating_e009: Then load files relative to that base:
t_page_guides_templating_e010: The loader sanitizes the path; if you absolutely need to bypass that (you usually don't), use load_unsafe.
t_page_guides_templating_e012: Build a context with whatever data the page needs:
t_page_guides_templating_e013: Lambdas are allowed and may themselves return strings containing mustache tags — the engine keeps parsing.
t_page_guides_templating_e015: Reuse fragments with the {{> partial.html }} syntax. The path is again relative to the global base. The docs site you're reading uses partials for the top nav, sidebar, TOC and footer.
t_page_guides_templating_e017: Render the page with the context and return the result:
t_page_guides_templating_e018: page.render(ctx) returns a crow::returnable with Content-Type set to text/html. Use render_string(ctx) if you'd rather have a plain std::string — for example when you want to embed the result inside another template.
t_page_guides_templating_e019: If your template needs to include literal {{ (for example a code sample for this very page), escape it with the HTML entities {{.
t_page_guides_testing_e002: You can exercise handlers directly without binding to a real port. Crow lets you call handle() on a synthetic request and inspect the response.
t_page_guides_testing_e005: For end-to-end coverage, start the app with run_async() and hit it with libcurl or any HTTP client:
t_page_guides_websockets_e002: WebSockets give you bidirectional, low-latency channels on the same port as your HTTP routes. Garvan exposes Crow's WebSocket API unchanged.
t_page_guides_websockets_e005: You'll typically want three handlers: onopen to track new connections, onmessage for incoming frames, and onclose to clean up state. Store connections in a thread-safe container if you need to broadcast.
t_page_home_desc: Garvan C++ — a fast, easy to use C++ web framework built on Crow.
t_page_home_e002: A fast, batteries-included C++23 web framework. Garvan extends Crow with an ORM, migrations, an event bus and job queue with a real SMTP mail job, a model/controller/service tier, and the kalpasan CLI — so you can ship HTTP, WebSocket, and background work without leaving C++.
t_page_home_e004: Built on Crow's high-performance core — routing is a compile-time decision tree.
t_page_home_e006: First-class drivers for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, MongoDB and MonetDB.
t_page_home_e008: Mustache templates, JSON, query builder, migrations, logger — out of the box.
t_page_home_e010: Real-time bidirectional communication with the same routing model as HTTP.
t_page_home_e012: Fire events, dispatch jobs, and send real HTML mail over SMTP with libcurl — all in-process.
t_page_home_e013: Get up and running in 8 lines
t_page_home_e014: Define a route, return a string, run the app. Garvan stays out of your way.
t_page_home_e016: Return a crow::json::wvalue from a handler and Garvan will set the right Content-Type for you. Garvan's own JsonValue wraps the same primitives for use inside services and models.
t_page_home_e018: A fluent query builder writes the SQL for any of the supported backends. Models extend OModel and expose find(), where() and relations.
t_page_home_e021: Start with the setup guide, then build your first endpoint.

t_page_privacy_e003: This page describes how the Garvan C++ documentation site handles your data. We aim to collect as little as possible — this is a static documentation site, not a service that profiles its visitors.
t_page_privacy_e005: We do not use third-party analytics, advertising trackers, or social-media beacons.
t_page_privacy_e006: We do not sell, share, or transmit your data to third parties.
t_page_privacy_e007: We do not require an account to read the documentation.
t_page_privacy_e008: We use one first-party cookie, solely to remember your preferred interface language.
t_page_privacy_e010: When you visit the site, the web server processes the standard information that every HTTP server receives in order to deliver a response:
t_page_privacy_e011: The IP address of the request (kept in the server's transient access log).
t_page_privacy_e012: The requested URL, HTTP method and status code.
t_page_privacy_e015: These access logs are used solely for operational purposes (debugging, abuse prevention, capacity planning) and are rotated and discarded on a short schedule. They are never combined with any other dataset and never used for profiling.
t_page_privacy_e016: The Garvan project itself — the C++ library you download and run on your own infrastructure — performs no telemetry, no “phone-home”, no usage reporting of any kind. The privacy policy on this page covers only the documentation website you are reading now.
t_page_privacy_e018: The site sets exactly one cookie:
t_page_privacy_e019: lang — stores your selected interface language (en, bg, ru, es, tr or pt). It is a first-party, SameSite=Lax cookie with a lifetime of one year. It contains no personal identifier.
t_page_privacy_e020: You may clear this cookie at any time from your browser's settings. The site will continue to work normally and will fall back to its default language.
t_page_privacy_e022: The documentation pages may link to external resources (such as GitHub, gnu.org, Crow's repository, or database vendor websites). When you click such a link, you leave this site and become subject to the third party's own privacy policy. We do not control and are not responsible for those policies.
t_page_privacy_e023: We do not embed third-party iframes, fonts, scripts or tracking pixels in the documentation pages.
t_page_privacy_e025: Because we do not maintain any personally identifiable record of you, there is no profile to access, correct, export or delete. If you believe a server-side access log contains information about you and you wish it to be removed, please reach out via the channel below.
t_page_privacy_e026: Depending on your jurisdiction, you may be entitled to additional rights under data-protection law (for example, the GDPR in the European Union or the UK GDPR in the United Kingdom). We will honour any reasonable request that is consistent with those frameworks.
t_page_privacy_e028: For privacy questions or requests, please open an issue on the project's GitHub tracker or use the contact details listed in the repository's README.md.
